heading: Q1
question:
A legal-tech startup builds a contract assistant. The assistant answers questions about 40,000 vendor contracts. Users ask questions like "What is the termination notice period in contract ACME-2024-118?". Users expect the exact clause quoted. The team designs the RAG pipeline. The team must choose a chunking strategy.

Constraint: answers must cite the exact clause. Small errors in clause text are unacceptable to the legal team.

Which chunking strategy best satisfies the constraint?

choices.A: Split each contract into 2,000-token chunks with no overlap, to keep each clause in rich surrounding context.
choices.B: Split each contract into 400 to 600-token chunks with 10 percent overlap, and attach contract ID plus section heading as metadata on every chunk.
choices.C: Embed each full contract as a single vector and retrieve the whole contract, letting the model find the clause.
choices.D: Chunk by fixed 100-token windows with no overlap or metadata, to maximize retrieval precision.

explanation:
Why B is correct: The constraint is exact clause citation. Small chunks raise retrieval precision. This ensures the cited clause is actually returned. Overlap prevents clauses split across boundaries from being lost. Metadata (contract ID, section) lets the system filter and cite correctly.
A is wrong. 2,000-token chunks dilute precision. The retriever returns long passages. The model may quote the wrong clause from the same chunk.
C is wrong. A whole contract far exceeds useful retrieval granularity. The model cannot reliably locate one clause in 40,000 embedded documents.
D is wrong. 100-token windows with no overlap will slice clauses in half. Without metadata, the system cannot attribute a quote to the right contract.

heading: Q2
question:
A sales team wants a Claude agent that can look up accounts and update opportunities in their CRM. The CRM exposes a stable, well-documented REST API with six endpoints. One engineer proposes building an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server; another proposes calling the REST API directly through function calling.

Constraint: ship in two weeks with the smallest maintenance surface. Only this one CRM is in scope.

Which integration approach should the architect choose?

choices.A: Call the CRM REST API directly through function calling, since there is one stable API and six endpoints.
choices.B: Build both an MCP server and direct REST tools, so the agent can choose at runtime.
choices.C: Use an agent-to-agent protocol so the CRM can negotiate with the Claude agent directly.
choices.D: Build an MCP server. MCP is the standard. Future tools will need MCP.

explanation:
Why A is correct: MCP pays off when there are many tools. It also pays off with dynamic discovery or shared servers across agents. With one stable API and a two-week deadline, direct function calling is simpler. It has less to maintain. This is exactly what the constraint asks for.
D is wrong. "MCP is the standard" is not a reason by itself. It adds a server to build, host, and secure. There is no capability gain here.
B is wrong. Maintaining two integration paths doubles the maintenance surface. This is the opposite of the constraint.
C is wrong. Agent-to-agent protocols connect agents to agents. They do not connect agents to a REST API. The CRM is not an agent.

heading: Q3
question:
A support agent got 47 tools. Every internal API got its own function. After launch, the team sees slow responses. The team sees frequent wrong-tool calls. The model often picks a similar tool. The model picks the wrong tool.

Then the model retries.

Constraint: reduce wrong-tool calls without removing any capability the agent needs.

What is the best fix?

choices.A: Upgrade to a larger model so it can handle 47 tools more reliably.
choices.B: Add five more helper tools that pre-select the right tool for common cases.
choices.C: Group tools into fewer, well-named functions (or namespaced MCP servers) so the agent sees a small set of distinct choices, with details revealed on demand.
choices.D: Raise the temperature so the agent explores different tools more creatively.

explanation:
Why C is correct: This is tool bloat. A flat list of 47 similar tools makes selection a guessing game. Grouping into a small set of distinct, well-named entry points cuts wrong-tool calls. It also keeps every capability reachable. This is progressive disclosure of the rest.
A is wrong. A larger model costs more. It also adds latency. It treats the symptom (bad selection) instead of the cause (47 indistinguishable options).
B is wrong. Adding tools makes the bloat worse. It does not make it better.
D is wrong. Higher temperature increases randomness. This increases wrong-tool calls.

heading: Q4
question:
An internal Claude agent reads and files expense reports through the finance API. It authenticates with a single shared service token that has full read and write access to every employee's expenses. A security review flags this before launch.

Constraint: the agent must act only within the requesting employee's own permissions. No shared privileged credential.

Which auth design resolves the finding?

choices.A: Remove authentication entirely and rely on the office VPN for access control.
choices.B: Keep the shared token but rotate it weekly.
choices.C: Give the agent one token per employee, all with full admin scope, stored in the agent's config file.
choices.D: Use OAuth 2.0 delegated tokens: each request carries the requesting user's own token, scoped to least privilege.

explanation:
Why D is correct: OAuth delegated tokens make the agent act as the user. The agent has only that user's permissions. This satisfies the least privilege principle. This removes the shared privileged credential.
B is wrong. Rotation does not change the blast radius. One leaked token still reaches everyone's expenses.
C is wrong. Per-employee admin tokens are still over-privileged. Storing them in a config file creates a new secret-sprawl problem.
A is wrong. The VPN proves network location. It does not prove user identity or authorization. Any user on the VPN can reach anyone's expenses.

heading: Q5
question:
A chat triage agent classifies incoming support tickets. The current design uses a large model with long chain-of-thought reasoning: accuracy is 93 percent, but p95 latency is 6 seconds. The product requirement is p95 latency under 2 seconds with accuracy at or above 90 percent. Ticket volume is 300,000 per month.

Constraint: p95 under 2 seconds AND accuracy at or above 90 percent. Both must hold at 300K tickets per month.

Which design best meets both bars?

choices.A: Route with a fast model first; escalate to the large model only when the fast model's confidence is low. Verify the mix on a labeled eval set.
choices.B: Cache every ticket classification so repeat tickets never hit the model.
choices.C: Switch everything to the smallest, fastest model and accept whatever accuracy results.
choices.D: Keep the large model but cut the output token limit in half to reduce latency.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Tiered routing gets most tickets under the latency bar. A fast model runs first. The system escalates tickets with low confidence. A large model protects the accuracy bar on hard cases. The eval-set check proves both bars hold before launch. This meets the constraint.
C is wrong. It guarantees the latency bar. It abandons the accuracy bar. "Accept whatever accuracy" violates the stated 90 percent floor.
D is wrong. Cutting output tokens does not reliably cut 6 seconds to under 2 seconds. It risks truncating the reasoning. The 93 percent accuracy depends on this reasoning.
B is wrong. Support tickets are mostly unique. Cache hit rates will be near zero. This changes almost nothing.

heading: Q6
question:
A production assistant handles 2 million requests per day across search, summarization, and tool calls. The team wants to detect quality drift, especially hallucinations, within one day of it starting. Today they only log the final user-facing text.

Constraint: detect hallucination drift within 24 hours at 2M requests per day, without storing every full prompt and completion (too expensive).

Which observability strategy fits?

choices.A: Emit structured traces (one span per tool call and model call with token counts and latency), sample a fraction of full transcripts, and run an automated faithfulness eval over the sample daily.
choices.B: Track only aggregate latency and token cost dashboards.
choices.C: Log only error responses and review them weekly.
choices.D: Store every prompt and completion in full, and hire reviewers to read them.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Structured traces give cheap, always-on coverage of behavior. Sampling keeps storage affordable at 2M requests per day. A daily automated faithfulness evaluation on the sample detects hallucination drift. This happens inside the 24-hour window.
C is wrong. Hallucinations rarely raise errors. Error logs miss them entirely. Weekly review misses the 24-hour window.
D is wrong. Full logging at 2M requests per day violates the cost constraint. Manual review cannot keep up.
B is wrong. Latency and cost dashboards say nothing about answer quality. Drift would be invisible.

heading: Q7
question:
An IT helpdesk agent handles two query patterns. Pattern (1): "find the three most similar past incidents to this error message" (fuzzy, wording varies). Pattern (2): "what is the status of incident INC-48210" (exact lookup by ID). The team now chooses a retrieval strategy over the incident database.

Constraint: both query patterns must return correct results. Fuzzy queries need semantic matching; exact queries must never return a "similar but wrong" incident.

Which two approaches together satisfy the constraint? (Select two.)

choices.A: Use dense vector search for both patterns, trusting the embedding to rank INC-48210 first.
choices.B: Route the query first: detect an incident ID pattern and send it to exact lookup, otherwise use semantic search.
choices.C: Use dense vector (semantic) search for the fuzzy similar-incident queries.
choices.D: Use exact keyword matching on the full error text for the fuzzy similar-incident queries, so results stay deterministic.

explanation:
Why C, B is correct: The constraint has two halves. C supplies the correct mechanism for the fuzzy half. This is dense semantic search. B supplies the routing rule. Detect an incident ID and send it to exact lookup. Otherwise, use semantic search.

Together they cover both query patterns. They use the correct mechanism each time.
D is wrong. Exact keyword matching cannot handle the fuzzy half. If the wording of the error varies, keyword lookup misses similar incidents. Semantic search would find these incidents. Determinism is not worth missed matches.
A is wrong. Semantic search can return a similar-but-wrong incident for an ID query. The constraint explicitly forbids this.

heading: Q8
question:
A team installs a community MCP server that gives their agent shell access. The server fetches its tool descriptions from a remote config file hosted by the server author. During testing, the agent suddenly tries to exfiltrate an API key after reading a tool description.

Constraint: the agent must be able to use third-party MCP servers without letting server content hijack its behavior.

What is the root cause, and the correct mitigation?

choices.A: Root cause: prompt injection through untrusted tool descriptions. Mitigation: treat MCP tool schemas as untrusted input, pin server versions, and sandbox or gate destructive tool calls behind confirmation.
choices.B: Root cause: the MCP protocol is insecure. Mitigation: stop using MCP and rewrite every tool by hand.
choices.C: Root cause: the API key was in the prompt. Mitigation: delete the key and continue.
choices.D: Root cause: the model is too small. Mitigation: upgrade the model.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Tool descriptions are model input. A malicious or compromised server can inject instructions through them. Pinning versions stops silent updates. Treating schemas as untrusted blocks the injection path. Sandboxing plus confirmation gates limit what a hijacked call can do.
D is wrong. Model size does not fix prompt injection. Larger models follow injected instructions just as well.
B is wrong. The protocol is not the flaw. Untrusted content is the flaw. Rewriting everything by hand removes MCP's value. It does not address the actual attack path.
C is wrong. Deleting the key after exfiltration does not stop the next attempt. It treats the symptom. It does not treat the injection.

heading: Q9
question:
A code-migration agent must work across a 2-million-line monorepo. The first design loaded a summary of every file into context at session start. Sessions now exceed the context window before the agent does any useful work, and costs have tripled.

Constraint: the agent must navigate the full repo without loading it all upfront, and per-session token cost must return to the original budget.

Which context strategy fixes this?

choices.A: Switch to a model with a 1-million-token context window and keep loading all summaries.
choices.B: Use progressive discovery. Give the agent search tools. Give the agent file-reading tools. Give the agent an index of entry points. The agent pulls only the code it needs. The agent pulls code when it needs it.
choices.C: Compress all summaries with a smaller model before the session starts, then load the compressed version.
choices.D: Split the repo into 50 fixed partitions and run 50 agents, one per partition.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Progressive discovery replaces the monolithic upfront load with on-demand retrieval. The agent starts from entry points. It fetches only relevant files. This fits any repo size. It brings token cost back down. This is the textbook fix for monolithic-context failure.
A is wrong. A bigger window just delays the failure. It costs more per token. It does not change the wasteful load-everything pattern.
C is wrong. Compression loses the details migration work depends on. This includes exact APIs and edge cases. It still front-loads cost for code never touched.
D is wrong. 50 agents multiply cost and coordination overhead. Most partitions are irrelevant to any single migration task.

heading: Q10
question:
A hospital uses a discharge-summary assistant. The assistant handles PHI. Legal requires patient data to stay in the hospital's AWS region. Legal requires no use of data for model training. Legal requires an audit of every access. The team considers the direct Anthropic API.

The team also considers Anthropic models on AWS Bedrock.

Constraint: data residency pinned to the hospital's approved AWS region, no training on PHI, full auditability. All three are legal requirements, not preferences.

Which deployment choice satisfies all three?

choices.A: Direct Anthropic API with zero data retention (ZDR) enabled, plus application-level audit logs.
choices.B: AWS Bedrock is in the hospital's region. It has a PHI-eligible configuration. It has a signed BAA. It sends inference logs to the hospital's audit store. No data leaves the region.
choices.C: Direct Anthropic API in the default configuration, since Anthropic never trains on API data by default.
choices.D: Self-host an open-weights model on hospital servers to avoid all third-party terms.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Bedrock keeps inference inside the chosen AWS region. This is residency. It offers HIPAA-eligible services with a BAA. This is the legal instrument auditors require. It lets the hospital own the audit logs. It is the only option that structurally satisfies all three legal requirements.
A is wrong. The direct API cannot pin processing and storage to a specific AWS region. Inference is global or US-only. Workspace storage is US-only. So, it cannot satisfy the residency requirement. ZDR plus a BAA would cover the other two requirements.

But residency is a hard legal bar here.
C is wrong. "Never trains by default" is a policy claim. It is not a regional control. It is not a contractual control. It fails residency. It fails auditability.
D is wrong. Self-hosting puts the whole compliance burden on the hospital. This includes hardening, patching, and auditing the model stack. It reduces model quality. It gives no legal gain over option B.

heading: Q11
question:
A company builds a RAG system over a mixed corpus: long PDF policy documents, relational tables of product specs, and a codebase. One engineer proposes a single chunking rule (500-token windows) and one dense vector index for everything.

Constraint: retrieval quality must stay high across all three content types. A query like "which products support feature X and what does the policy say about refunds" must work.

Why will the single-strategy proposal fail, and what should replace it?

choices.A: It will not fail. Uniform chunking is the industry standard for mixed corpora.
choices.B: It will fail on cost. Replace it with a smaller embedding model.
choices.C:
It will fail. Different data shapes need different handling. Chunk PDFs by section. Index tables as structured rows with metadata filters. Chunk code by function. Use hybrid dense plus keyword search.

Do this over the combined index.
choices.D: It will fail on latency. Replace it with an in-memory cache of all embeddings.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Tables sliced into 500-token windows destroy row structure. Code sliced mid-function destroys meaning. Match the chunking to the data shape. This includes sections, rows, and functions. Use metadata filters and hybrid search. This keeps what each type needs for accurate retrieval.
B is wrong. The failure is retrieval quality. It is not embedding cost. A cheaper embedding of badly chunked text is still badly chunked.
D is wrong. Latency is not the problem. A cache does not repair broken chunk boundaries.
A is wrong. It denies the problem. Uniform chunking across prose, tables, and code is a known retrieval-quality trap.

heading: Q12
question:
A travel company has two vendor-built agents: a booking agent (flights and hotels) and an expense agent (receipts and policy). They must cooperate: after booking, the booking agent hands trip details to the expense agent, which files the report. An architect must choose the integration mechanism between them.

Constraint: the two agents are separate systems from different vendors. They must exchange goals and status, not just raw data.

Which mechanism fits, and why?

choices.A: A shared REST API that both agents poll for updates.
choices.B: An agent-to-agent protocol, because the integration is agent to agent: they need to delegate tasks and report status, which is what agent-to-agent communication is for.
choices.C: Merge both agents into one agent with all tools, eliminating the integration.
choices.D: MCP, because MCP connects the booking agent's tools to the expense agent.

explanation:
Why B is correct: MCP connects agents to tools and data sources. It does not define how two autonomous agents delegate and coordinate. An agent-to-agent protocol is for this purpose. It handles task handoff, status updates, and negotiation between separate agents.
D is wrong. It misapplies MCP. MCP is agent-to-tool. It is not agent-to-agent.
A is wrong. Polling a REST API gives data exchange. It gives no task-delegation semantics. Each vendor would have to invent coordination.
C is wrong. The agents are separate vendor systems. Merging them is not technically feasible. Merging them is not contractually feasible.

heading: Q13
question:
An accounting firm processes 20,000 vendor invoices each month. The steps are fixed. The steps are known. Extract fields. Validate totals against the PO. Flag mismatches.

Post to the ledger. The sequence does not change for any invoice.

Constraint: the process is fully deterministic in structure. Auditability of every step matters more than flexibility.

Which architectural pattern fits best?

choices.A: An augmented LLM with open tool access and no prescribed sequence.
choices.B: A multi-agent swarm where subagents negotiate who handles each invoice.
choices.C: A fully agentic system where the model plans its own steps per invoice.
choices.D: A workflow: fixed prompt chain with defined steps, validation gates, and logging at each stage.

explanation:
Why D is correct: The steps are known upfront. The steps never change. A workflow is the most reliable choice. It is also the most auditable choice. It removes the nondeterminism that the constraint does not want.
C is wrong. Agentic planning adds nondeterminism. It adds cost to a process. The steps of this process are already known. Flexibility is not necessary here.
A is wrong. Open tool access without a prescribed sequence makes auditing harder. It invites skipped validation steps.
B is wrong. A negotiating swarm is massive overengineering. This is for identical invoices with fixed steps.

heading: Q14
question:
A CFO decides whether to fund a Claude-based contract review assistant. The vendor talks about "AI transformation." The vendor talks about "delighting users." The CFO asks for the business case in her language.

Constraint: The case must show measurable business value. It must not show technology enthusiasm.

How should the architect frame the value?

choices.A: Map the solution to value pillars with numbers: hours saved per contract, cost per review before and after, error-rate reduction, and payback period.
choices.B: Promise full transformation of the legal department within one quarter.
choices.C: Focus on the elegant multi-agent architecture under the hood.
choices.D: Emphasize that the system uses the most advanced model available.

explanation:
Why A is correct: The value pillars are efficiency, cost, productivity, and performance. The CFO's language is numbers. This includes hours, cost per unit, error rates, and payback. A translates the solution into these terms.
D is wrong. Model choice is an implementation detail. It is not business value.
B is wrong. An unmeasurable transformation promise is the hype. The CFO screens out this hype.
C is wrong. Architecture elegance does not appear on any value pillar.

heading: Q15
question:
A market-research team wants a 30-page industry report generated from 200 source documents. A single prompt ("write the report") produces shallow, repetitive output that misses key sources.

Constraint: the report must synthesize all 200 sources with depth in each section.

Which decomposition approach fixes the shallow output?

choices.A: Reduce the source set to 20 documents so one prompt can handle it.
choices.B: Use a larger context window and repeat the same single prompt.
choices.C: Decompose: a planner outlines sections, researcher subagents gather evidence per section in parallel, then a synthesizer writes the full report from the gathered evidence.
choices.D: Ask the model to write the report one page at a time with no plan.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Decomposition matches the work to the model's strengths. First, plan the structure. Then, gather evidence for each section in parallel. After that, synthesize the information. Each step has a manageable context. This avoids one impossible large prompt.
B is wrong because a bigger window does not fix the lack of structure. The model still skims. It does not go deep.
D is wrong because writing page-by-page without a plan produces incoherent reports. The reports drift from the outline.
A is wrong because it discards 90 percent of the sources. This violates the synthesis constraint.

heading: Q16
question:
A competitive-intelligence system uses one orchestrator and six researcher subagents covering pricing, product, hiring, patents, news, and social. Early tests show subagents overwriting each other's findings and two agents researching the same competitor twice.

Constraint: each finding recorded once, no duplicated research effort, and the orchestrator can see everything.

Which orchestration design resolves this?

choices.A: Run the six researchers sequentially so they cannot collide.
choices.B: Give every subagent its own private memory and merge by concatenating outputs.
choices.C: Let subagents coordinate peer-to-peer with a shared chat channel.
choices.D: Orchestrator assigns non-overlapping scopes, all findings go to a shared structured store with unique keys, and the orchestrator merges at the end.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Non-overlapping scopes remove duplicated effort. A shared keyed store prevents overwrites. Each finding has one key. The orchestrator keeps full visibility for the merge. All three parts of the constraint are met.
C is wrong. Peer-to-peer chat is not structured. Agents still collide. The orchestrator loses visibility into side conversations.
A is wrong because sequential execution fixes collisions. It does this by destroying parallelism. Six researchers take six times longer.
B is wrong because private memories plus concatenation duplicates effort. It produces conflicting merged output. There is no deduplication.

heading: Q17
question:
A support team deploys an answer bot and adds a thumbs up / thumbs down button on every answer. After three months they have 40,000 ratings but answer quality has not improved. The ratings sit in a database nobody queries.

Constraint: user feedback must actually drive quality improvement, on a repeating cadence.

What is not present? What completes the process?

choices.A: More ratings. Add a popup asking every user to rate.
choices.B: This is a feedback loop. Sample low-rated answers each week. Add the failures to the eval set. Review prompt or retrieval fixes against the eval set. Ship what makes the score better.
choices.C: A bigger model, since ratings show the current one is weak.
choices.D: Delete the rating button; it creates noise without value.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Feedback makes quality better only when it goes somewhere. Failures become evaluation cases. You test fixes against the evaluation set. The loop repeats on a schedule. B builds the full input, processing, output, and feedback system. The constraint asks for this.
A is wrong because the problem is not rating volume. 40,000 unused ratings prove more data without a loop changes nothing.
C is wrong because the ratings do not diagnose the model as the cause. The failures can be retrieval or prompt issues. A bigger model would share these issues.
D is wrong because it destroys the signal. It does not use the signal.

heading: Q18
question:
A team builds a code-review bot. It runs the linter. It runs the test suite. It reads the diff. It posts review comments. The sequence is always the same.

Writing the comments is the only open-ended part. One architect calls it "agentic." Another calls it "a workflow with tools."

Constraint: choose the pattern honestly so the team designs the right controls (and does not overbuild).

Which pattern is this, and why does the label matter?

choices.A:
This is an Augmented LLM. It is a workflow with tools. The path is fixed. The model fills in one open-ended step. The label is important. A fixed path needs validation gates.

It does not need agent loop controls.
choices.B: Fully manual, because a human must approve every comment.
choices.C: Multi-agent, because linting, testing, and commenting are three jobs.
choices.D: Agentic, because it uses tools. Agentic systems need loop limits and escalation controls.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Tool use alone does not make a system agentic. Who decides the steps is important. Here the steps are fixed. So, it is an augmented LLM. It is a tool-using workflow. The label controls the system.
Truly agentic loops need iteration limits and stop conditions.
D is wrong because it mislabels the system. Applying agent loop controls to a fixed pipeline adds complexity. It does this without benefit.
B is wrong because human approval of every comment defeats the automation goal. The design does not require this.
C is wrong because three sequential steps do not make three agents. Splitting them adds orchestration overhead. There is no gain.

heading: Q19
question:
A trading desk wants a Claude assistant for pre-trade research. The desk's SLA: 99.9 percent uptime, p95 response under 3 seconds, including during market-open spikes when request volume jumps 10x.

Constraint: the SLA must hold during 10x spikes. A slow or down assistant during market open is worse than no assistant.

Which design best protects the SLA?

choices.A: Use the largest model for best answer quality and accept slower spikes.
choices.B: Disable the assistant during market open to protect the SLA.
choices.C: Provision for average load and add a queue; users wait during spikes.
choices.D: Design for peak with autoscaling. Add a defined degraded mode. Use cached or short answers. Show a clear banner when the full pipeline cannot meet 3 seconds. The SLA states degraded-mode behavior clearly.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Autoscaling handles the 10x spike. The explicit degraded mode means the SLA is honest. It states what happens under extreme load. It does not silently break. Stating degraded behavior in the SLA makes it a real SLA. It is not just a hope.
C is wrong because queuing during market open directly violates the 3-second p95 requirement.
A is wrong because it prioritizes quality over the stated SLA. The constraint ranks the latency bar above model size.
B is wrong because disabling the system at peak need is an admission. It means the design failed the SLA.

heading: Q20
question:
An insurer designs a claims pipeline: intake (classify claim type), processing (validate against policy, estimate payout), output (draft decision letter), feedback (adjuster corrections flow back into the eval set). The architect must present the end-to-end design.

Constraint: every stage must be observable, and failures at any stage must be routable to a human without losing the claim.

Which design element is most critical to satisfying the constraint?

choices.A: Making the pipeline fully autonomous with no human queues, to maximize throughput.
choices.B: Combining intake and processing into one giant prompt to reduce handoff errors.
choices.C: Using the same model for all four stages to keep behavior consistent.
choices.D: Stage boundaries with structured handoffs: each stage emits a typed result plus confidence. Route low-confidence or failed results to a human queue. Attach the full stage history to each routed result. Log every handoff.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Structured handoffs with confidence scores make each stage observable. The human queue with full history satisfies the routability requirement. It does not lose claims. Logging every handoff gives the audit trail. It is the only option built around the constraint.
C is wrong. Model uniformity does not create observability or human routing. It is an implementation convenience.
A is wrong. It directly violates the human-routing half of the constraint.
B is wrong. Merging stages destroys per-stage observability. It makes failures harder to localize.

heading: Q21
question:
A localization team must translate 5,000 product documents (each 20 to 80 pages) into 12 languages. Quality must be consistent across languages, terminology must match the company glossary, and the job must finish in 30 days.

Constraint: glossary-consistent terminology across all 12 languages, 30-day deadline, no quality drift between early and late documents.

Which orchestration strategy best meets all three?

choices.A: One agent translating documents sequentially in all 12 languages.
choices.B: Split documents into sections. Translate sections at the same time for each language. Inject the glossary into every prompt. A hierarchical merge step checks cross-section consistency. Then finalize each document.
choices.C: Twelve separate agents, one per language, each working independently with no shared glossary.
choices.D: Machine-translate everything first, then have one agent proofread all 5,000 documents.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Parallel fan-out meets the 30-day deadline. Glossary injection in every prompt enforces terminology consistency. The hierarchical merge catches the cross-section drift that parallel work introduces. Each constraint maps to one design element.
A is wrong. Sequential translation of 5,000 documents times 12 languages cannot fit 30 days.
C is wrong. Independent agents with no shared glossary guarantee terminology drift across languages.
D is wrong. One proofreading agent over 5,000 documents reintroduces the sequential bottleneck. The deadline fails.

heading: Q22
question:
A CIO has budget for one AI initiative. Proposal X: automate invoice data entry (saves 4,000 staff-hours per year, measurable in 3 months, low risk). Proposal Y: an AI product copilot for customers (could open a new revenue line, 12-month horizon, high uncertainty). The company's stated strategy this year is cost discipline.

Constraint: the pick must align with the stated strategy (cost discipline) and be defensible with measurable value.

Which two statements best guide the decision? (Select two.)

choices.A: Fund both at half budget to keep options open.
choices.B: Choose X: it maps to the efficiency and cost pillars, matches the cost-discipline strategy, and its value is measurable within one quarter.
choices.C: Choose Y: transformation projects always beat efficiency projects in the long run.
choices.D: Defer the decision until both proposals have quantified value, cost, risk, and time-to-value estimates.

explanation:
Why B, D is correct: B and D work as a pair. B names the strategy-aligned pick. X maps to the efficiency and cost pillars. It is measurable within a quarter. This is what the constraint demands. D states the evidentiary standard that makes the pick defensible.
It requires quantified value, cost, risk, and time-to-value for both proposals. X already meets that standard. Y does not. This is exactly why X wins.
C is wrong. "Transformation always beats efficiency" is a slogan. It is not an analysis. It ignores the stated strategy. It ignores the measurability constraint.
A is wrong. Splitting the budget starves both proposals. It avoids the prioritization decision that the CIO needs.

heading: Q23
question:
Give a research agent open-ended questions. An example is "what should our pricing strategy be?" The agent sometimes loops during testing. It calls the same search tools many times. It refines forever. It never makes the final memo. Each loop uses many tokens.

Constraint: the agent must always terminate with a useful deliverable, and runaway token burn must be impossible.

Which control design guarantees termination?

choices.A: Tell the agent in the system prompt to "be efficient and finish promptly."
choices.B: Use hard controls. Set a maximum iteration budget. Use an explicit stop condition. The agent must satisfy a deliverable checklist. Escalate to a human with partial results. Do this when the budget is gone.
choices.C: Remove all search tools so the agent cannot loop on them.
choices.D: Lower the temperature to zero so the agent behaves deterministically.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Prompt instructions alone do not guarantee termination. A hard iteration budget makes runaway burn impossible. The deliverable checklist defines "done." This allows the agent to stop. Human escalation with partial results guarantees a useful output.
A is wrong. Polite prompt requests are soft controls. The observed looping happened despite similar instructions.
C is wrong. Removing search tools cripples the research task. The agent exists to do this task.
D is wrong. Temperature zero does not prevent loops. A deterministic agent can deterministically repeat the same calls.

heading: Q24
question:
A team builds a meeting-summarization feature. The product requirement is that summaries must not invent action items that were never discussed. The team currently measures quality with ROUGE scores against reference summaries.

Constraint: the metric must capture invented content (hallucinated action items), which is the actual product risk.

What should the primary metric be?

choices.A: Latency, since fast summaries matter most to users.
choices.B: ROUGE score, since it is the standard summarization metric.
choices.C: Faithfulness: the share of summary claims verifiable against the transcript, rated by humans on a sample plus an automated claim-check.
choices.D: Summary length in words, since shorter summaries hallucinate less.

explanation:
Why C is correct: The product risk: invented action items. ROUGE measures word overlap. It does not measure truthfulness. Faithfulness directly measures whether the transcript grounds each claim. This is exactly the constraint.
B is wrong. ROUGE rewards similar wording. A fluent invented action item can score well on ROUGE.
D is wrong. Length is not a quality metric. Short summaries can still invent content.
A is wrong. Latency measures speed. It says nothing about invented action items.

heading: Q25
question:
A bank builds an eval set for its loan-document assistant. An engineer suggests 50 examples pulled from last week's tickets. The assistant must handle 12 document types, including rare ones like foreign income statements.

Constraint: The eval set must show all 12 document types. This includes rare types. If not, launch metrics will mislead.

How should the eval set be built?

choices.A: Skip the eval set and rely on production user ratings after launch.
choices.B: Use the 50 recent tickets; recent data is the most representative.
choices.C: Build a stratified set. Sample across all 12 document types. Use minimum counts per type. Include rare types and known edge cases. Size the set in the hundreds.
choices.D: Generate 50 synthetic examples with another model; it is faster.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Stratified sampling guarantees coverage of every document type. This includes rare types. This is the constraint. Fifty recent tickets will over-represent common types. They will hide failures on the rare types.
B is wrong. Recency does not equal coverage. Rare types will be absent. Their failures will be invisible.
D is wrong. Synthetic examples reflect the generating model's biases. They do not reflect real document variety.
A is wrong. Post-launch ratings mean shipping untested. The constraint is about pre-launch confidence.

heading: Q26
question:
After a prompt rewrite, the support bot's answers get noticeably worse: more off-topic replies, more "I cannot help with that" on in-scope questions. The team debates whether the prompt caused it or something else changed.

Constraint: determine whether the prompt change caused the regression, with evidence, before changing anything else.

What is the correct first diagnostic step?

choices.A: Ask users whether they noticed a change.
choices.B: Immediately revert the prompt; the timing proves it caused the problem.
choices.C: Run the frozen eval set against both the old and new prompts and compare scores per category.
choices.D: Switch to a larger model to compensate for the weaker prompt.

explanation:
Why C is correct: A frozen eval set runs against both prompt versions. This isolates the prompt as the variable. Per-category comparison shows exactly what regressed. This gives evidence instead of a guess.
B is wrong. Timing is correlation. It is not evidence. Reverting without diagnosis teaches nothing. It may discard a fixable improvement.
D is wrong. It compensates blindly without confirming the cause. It raises cost permanently.
A is wrong. User impressions are noisy and slow. The eval set gives a same-day answer.

heading: Q27
question:
A team wants to A/B test a new support-bot prompt in production. The bot serves 100,000 conversations per week across three regions with different question mixes. The team plans to run the new prompt for one week, then the old prompt for the next week, and compare.

Constraint: the comparison must be fair: same traffic mix, no time-based confounds, and guardrail metrics watched alongside the primary metric.

What is wrong with the planned test, and what is the correct design?

choices.A: Sequential weeks confound the prompt with time (different weeks bring different question mixes). Run both prompts concurrently on randomly split traffic, pre-register the primary metric plus guardrail metrics (safety, latency), and require a minimum sample before calling a winner.
choices.B: The test needs more regions, not a different design.
choices.C: Skip the test and ship the new prompt; offline evals already passed.
choices.D: Nothing is wrong; sequential weeks are a valid A/B test.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Concurrent randomized split removes time confounds. The traffic mix is identical. Pre-registration prevents cherry-picking metrics after the fact. Guardrail metrics catch regressions that the primary metric misses. Every element answers the constraint.
D is wrong. Sequential weeks let external changes masquerade as prompt effects. These changes include product launches and news events.
B is wrong. More regions do not fix the time confound. The design flaw is structural.
C is wrong. Offline evaluations do not cover production distribution shift. The constraint demands a fair live comparison.

heading: Q28
question:
A legal research assistant sometimes cites court cases that do not exist. The citations look plausible: real-sounding names, correct formats, wrong reality. The team needs to diagnose the failure mode and fix it.

Constraint: no fabricated citation may reach the user. The fix must be verifiable, not just "a better prompt."

Which diagnosis and fix pair is correct?

choices.A: Diagnosis: prompt failure. Fix: add "do not hallucinate" to the system prompt.
choices.B: Diagnosis: ungrounded generation. The model invents citations from parametric memory. Fix: require every citation to resolve against the retrieved sources (citation-to-source verification step). Eval with a groundedness metric that checks each cited case exists in the corpus.
choices.C: Diagnosis: model mismatch. Fix: switch to a larger model.
choices.D: Diagnosis: bad luck. Fix: retry failed answers up to three times.

explanation:
Why B is correct: The failure: ungrounded generation. This is a hallucination subtype. The verifiable fix is structural. Citations must resolve to retrieved sources. The evaluation metric checks existence in the corpus. A prompt plea is not verifiable.
A verification step is verifiable.
A is wrong. "Do not hallucinate" is not a control. You cannot verify it. Models still confabulate under it.
C is wrong. Larger models also hallucinate citations from parametric memory. Scale does not ground outputs.
D is wrong. Retries sample the same ungrounded distribution. They do not add grounding.

heading: Q29
question:
A document-processing pipeline handles 10 million tokens per day. Finance mandates a 40 percent cost cut next quarter. Current accuracy is 94 percent on the eval set, and the SLA floor is 90 percent. The pipeline uses a large model for every document with a 4,000-token system prompt repeated on each call.

Constraint: cut cost 40 percent while staying at or above 90 percent accuracy.

Which optimization plan best fits?

choices.A: Reduce the eval set size so accuracy is cheaper to measure.
choices.B: Switch everything to the cheapest model and hope accuracy holds.
choices.C: Cache the repeated 4,000-token system prompt. Use a smaller model for the easy document tier. Verify the smaller model on the eval set. Use shorter output limits. Re-run the eval set. Confirm accuracy stays above 90 percent.
choices.D: Process documents only on weekdays to cut volume 28 percent.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Caching attacks the repeated-prefix waste directly. Tiering moves easy work to cheaper models. It does not touch hard cases. The evaluation re-run proves the 90 percent floor still holds. Cost drops on three fronts. You verify accuracy.

It is not hoped for.
B is wrong. "Hope accuracy holds" violates the verified-accuracy half of the constraint.
D is wrong. It cuts service. It does not cut cost efficiency. Weekend documents still need processing.
A is wrong. Shrinking the evaluation set hides regressions. It changes the measurement. It does not change the cost.

heading: Q30
question:
Every call to a classification API includes the same 4,000-token system prompt. The system prompt has a role, rules, and 12 few-shot examples. A short user message follows the system prompt. This repeated prefix uses most tokens. The system prompt changes about one time each month.

Constraint: cut token cost on the repeated prefix without changing model behavior.

What is the right optimization?

choices.A: Batch 100 user messages per call to amortize the prefix.
choices.B: Delete the few-shot examples to shorten the prompt.
choices.C: Enable prompt caching on the stable prefix. The system bills it one time. The system reuses it across calls.
choices.D: Switch to a model with cheaper input tokens but different behavior.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Prompt caching is for this purpose. It reuses a long stable prefix across calls. The system processes the prefix one time. The system caches the prefix. This cuts cost. It does not change behavior.
B is wrong. Deleting examples changes behavior. It likely changes accuracy. The constraint forbids behavior change.
D is wrong. A different model changes behavior by definition.
A is wrong. Batching changes latency characteristics. It risks cross-contamination between messages. It is a workaround. It is not the purpose-built fix.

heading: Q31
question:
A team evaluates a code-generation agent with a single metric: unit-test pass rate on 300 tasks. The agent scores 82 percent. In pilot, developers complain the code is unreadable, ignores project conventions, and sometimes passes tests while solving the wrong problem.

Constraint: the eval must reflect real developer acceptance, not just test passage.

Which two additions fix the eval blind spots? (Select two.)

choices.A: An LLM-judge review scoring code readability and convention adherence against the project style guide.
choices.B: Human spot-checks on a sample, rating whether the code actually solves the requested problem.
choices.C: More unit tests, raising the set from 300 to 3,000 tasks.
choices.D: Measuring tokens per task to reward efficiency.

explanation:
Why A, B is correct: The blind spots are readability and conventions. A LLM judge checks against the style guide. This scales across all tasks (A). Wrong-problem solutions can still pass tests. Humans verify intent match on a sample (B). This is mixed-methodology evaluation.
It uses automated functional tests, a judge, and human review. Each covers what the others miss.
C is wrong. More of the same metric does not fix the metric's blind spots. 3,000 pass-rate tests still ignore readability and intent.
D is wrong. Token efficiency is not related to the complaints. Optimizing it can even reward terse, unreadable code.

heading: Q32
question:
A due-diligence agent reads deal documents up to 180,000 tokens. The team chose a model with a 200,000-token window, assuming it handles the full length. In testing, accuracy on facts buried past the 100,000-token mark drops sharply, even though everything fits in the window.

Constraint: facts anywhere in the 180K document must be found with uniform reliability.

What is the diagnosis and the fix?

choices.A: Diagnosis: prompt failure. Fix: add "pay attention to the end of the document" to the prompt.
choices.B: Diagnosis: the documents are too long. Fix: truncate to 100,000 tokens.
choices.C: Diagnosis: advertised context length is not effective context length; attention degrades on distant content ("lost in the middle" and late-position decay). Fix: retrieve-then-read (pull the relevant sections first, then reason over a small focused context), and eval accuracy at each position band.
choices.D: Diagnosis: the model is defective. Fix: wait for the next model release.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Fitting in the window does not mean the model uses the whole window well. This is the known effective-vs-advertised context gap. Retrieve-then-read shrinks the reasoning context. It shrinks it to the relevant sections. This restores uniform reliability. Position-banded evaluations prove this.
B is wrong. Truncation deletes the facts. The constraint requires finding these facts.
D is wrong. The behavior is a known property of long-context models. It is not a defect in one release.
A is wrong. A prompt plea does not repair attention decay. This decay occurs over 180,000 tokens.

heading: Q33
question:
A customer-facing agent has a strict policy: it must never reveal system instructions, even under jailbreak attempts. The team wants production monitoring that detects successful prompt-injection attacks, not just attempts.

Constraint: detect successful injections (instructions actually leaked) within hours, at high traffic volume, with a low false-positive rate.

Which monitoring design works?

choices.A: Log all conversations and have analysts read them daily.
choices.B: Block any user message containing the word "system."
choices.C: Keyword search for "ignore previous instructions" in user messages; alert on every match.
choices.D:
Train an output-side classifier. The classifier detects leaked system content. Run the classifier over sampled completions. Plant canary tokens in the system prompt. The appearance of canary tokens in outputs proves a leak. Alert on classifier hits.

Alert on canary sightings.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Attempts are input-side and noisy. Success is output-side. The classifier detects leaked content in outputs. Canary tokens give near-zero-false-positive proof of a leak. Sampling keeps it affordable at volume. Detection happens within hours.
C is wrong. It detects attempts, not successes. Attackers constantly rephrase. False positives flood the team.
A is wrong. Manual review cannot cover high volume. It cannot cover it within hours.
B is wrong. It blocks legitimate messages. For example, "my system is down." It misses rephrased attacks.

heading: Q34
question:
A support agent sometimes pastes customers' full credit-card numbers into its replies when quoting past tickets. The compliance team requires that no full card number ever appears in any agent output.

Constraint: The output must not show full card numbers. The control must work. The control must work even if the model asks for the number.

Which guardrail design satisfies the constraint?

choices.A: Add "never share card numbers" to the system prompt.
choices.B: Redact card numbers from the retrieved context. Do this before the numbers reach the model. This is input minimization. Use a deterministic output filter. This filter blocks or masks card number patterns. Do this before the system sends the reply.
choices.C: Train the support team to not ask about card numbers.
choices.D: Log all outputs and review them at the end of each week.

explanation:
Why B is correct: A prompt request is bypassable. The constraint needs structural controls. Input minimization means the model often does not see the number. The deterministic output filter catches what slips through. Two independent layers make "zero" achievable.
A is wrong. User instructions can override prompt instructions. This is not a guarantee.
C is wrong. It controls the humans. It does not control the agent's outputs under adversarial input.
D is wrong. Weekly review detects leaks days late. The constraint is prevention. It is not after-the-fact detection.

heading: Q35
question:
A bank uses a Claude agent. The agent drafts loan decisions. It can approve, deny, or refer. Regulators require human review for denials.

A human must review every denial. A human must sign off on every denial. Do this before the denial reaches the applicant. There are no exceptions.

Which human-in-the-loop design complies?

choices.A: The agent issues denials directly but logs them for audit.
choices.B: The agent issues decisions directly; humans review a 5 percent sample afterward.
choices.C: The agent drafts every decision. It attaches its reasoning. Approvals can auto-issue below a risk threshold. Every denial waits in a queue. A human reviews and signs off on every denial.
choices.D: Humans write the decisions and the agent only formats them.

explanation:
Why C is correct: The constraint stops denials. Each denial needs human sign-off. Do this before delivery. The agent attaches the reasoning. This makes the review informed. Approvals below a risk threshold can flow through.

It does not change the constraint.
B is wrong. Sampling lets 95 percent of denials through unreviewed. This violates "no exceptions."
D is wrong. It removes the agent's value. The constraint needs human review of denials. It does not need human authorship of everything.
A is wrong. Logging is not review. The denial still reaches the applicant unreviewed.

heading: Q36
question:
A DevOps agent has a tool. The tool can delete cloud resources. In a test, a misread instruction caused a problem. The agent deleted a staging database. The team must keep the delete capability. This capability is necessary for cleanup work.

The team must make accidents structurally unlikely.

Constraint: keep the delete tool, but a single model mistake must never cause an irreversible deletion.

Which control set meets the constraint?

choices.A: A system prompt telling the agent to "be very careful with deletions."
choices.B: Rate-limit the delete tool to one call per hour.
choices.C: Remove the delete tool and do all deletions manually.
choices.D: A confirmation gate is for destructive calls. A human or a second approval is necessary. A dry-run preview shows what the system will delete. Least-privilege scopes prevent the tool from touching production databases.

explanation:
Why D is correct: There are three independent layers. The confirmation gate stops a single mistake from executing. The dry-run shows the blast radius before action. Least-privilege scopes contain what the tool can reach. These layers together make one mistake insufficient for disaster.
C is wrong. It deletes the capability the team needs. It does not control the capability.
A is wrong. Prompt wording is not a structural control. Mistakes still execute.
B is wrong. Rate limiting slows accidents. It does not stop the one wrong deletion.

heading: Q37
question:
A European retailer deploys a Claude shopping assistant for EU customers. It stores conversation logs (which may contain names, addresses, and order details) for quality review. The legal team requires GDPR compliance, including the right to erasure.

Constraint: honor erasure requests fully, and never use customer conversations for model training.

Which two measures are necessary? Select two measures.

choices.A: A signed data processing agreement with the model provider, plus zero data retention (or documented non-training) terms.
choices.B: An erasure pipeline: find all stored copies of a user's data (logs, eval samples, backups) and delete them on request within the legal deadline.
choices.C: Anonymize all analytics dashboards shown to executives.
choices.D: Store the logs in the cheapest available region.

explanation:
Why A, B is correct: A covers the provider side. It includes contractual non-training terms. It also includes a DPA. GDPR needs the DPA for processors. B covers the company's own side. Erasure is not useful if backups and evaluation samples keep copies.

Each addresses a different part of the constraint.
C is good hygiene. It does not satisfy either part of the constraint. Dashboards are not the erasure problem. They are not the training problem.
D is wrong and risky. The cheapest region can be outside the EU. This creates a data-residency problem. It adds to other problems.

heading: Q38
question:
A clinic makes a triage assistant. The assistant reads patient messages. The messages contain PHI. The assistant suggests urgency levels to nurses. The compliance officer asks what is necessary before PHI touches the system.

Constraint: PHI can only flow through HIPAA-eligible services. The services must have proper agreements. The system can only use the minimum necessary data.

What is the minimum compliant setup?

choices.A: Any model API works as long as the app encrypts traffic with HTTPS.
choices.B: A HIPAA-eligible deployment (for example Anthropic models on Bedrock or Vertex with HIPAA-eligible configuration), a signed BAA (business associate agreement), minimum-necessary data collection, and audit logging of PHI access.
choices.C: On-premise servers only; cloud providers can never handle PHI.
choices.D: Patient consent forms, with no other technical measures needed.

explanation:
Why B is correct: HIPAA needs the legal instrument (BAA). It needs the eligible service configuration. It needs the minimum-necessary standard. It needs auditability. B is the complete minimum set. Each element maps to a specific HIPAA requirement.
A is wrong. HTTPS is necessary. It is not sufficient. It provides no BAA. It provides no eligibility. It provides no audit trail.
C is wrong. HIPAA-eligible cloud configurations exist for this purpose. On-prem is not a legal requirement.
D is wrong. Consent does not replace the BAA. It does not replace safeguards. It does not replace minimum-necessary requirements.

heading: Q39
question:
A company pilots an agent that screens job applications and ranks candidates for interviews. Early results show candidates from certain universities ranked consistently higher, and the team worries about bias.

Constraint: screening must be fair and demonstrably so: decisions traceable to job-relevant criteria, with disparate impact measured, not assumed away.

Which design best addresses the fairness concern?

choices.A: Add more training data so the model becomes fair on its own.
choices.B: Remove university names from the inputs, keep everything else the same, and ship.
choices.C: Do a structured evaluation. Hide identifying details. Score each candidate against a fixed job-relevant rubric. Log the rubric scores as the decision record. Run disparate-impact analysis across demographic groups before launch.
choices.D: Use the agent only for scheduling interviews, never for ranking.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Blinding removes the obvious proxy. The fixed rubric forces job-relevant criteria. Logged scores make decisions auditable. Disparate-impact analysis verifies fairness with data. It does not use assumptions. It is the only option that is demonstrable.
B is wrong. Proxies survive blinding. These include wording, employment gaps, and zip codes. You cannot know it worked without measurement.
D is wrong. It abandons the use case. It does not make the use case fair.
A is wrong. More data does not de-bias a model. It can entrench existing patterns.

heading: Q40
question:
A federal agency wants a Claude document assistant for internal analysts. Procurement requires FedRAMP authorization for any cloud service handling the data. The team proposes the direct Anthropic API because "it is simpler."

Constraint: the deployment must satisfy FedRAMP authorization requirements. Simplicity does not override procurement rules.

What should the architect recommend?

choices.A: Run the assistant on analysts' laptops to avoid cloud authorization entirely.
choices.B: Proceed with the direct API; FedRAMP applies to infrastructure, not AI APIs.
choices.C:
Deploy through a FedRAMP-authorized route. Use Claude for Government. This is Anthropic's FedRAMP High authorized platform. Or use Anthropic models via AWS Bedrock GovCloud. Or use Vertex AI Assured Workloads. Add compliant audit logging.

Document the authorization boundary.
choices.D: Self-attest that the direct API meets FedRAMP controls and file the attestation.

explanation:
Why C is correct: FedRAMP authorization attaches to the service boundary. Claude for Government carries Anthropic's own FedRAMP High authorization. The Bedrock GovCloud and Vertex AI Assured Workloads routes inherit their clouds' authorizations. The audit logging plus boundary documentation is what assessors actually check.
B is wrong. The commercial direct API is not FedRAMP authorized. Anthropic's FedRAMP High authorization applies to Claude for Government, a separate platform. AI APIs handling agency data are in scope. "Simpler" is not an authorization.
D is wrong. Self-attestation is not FedRAMP authorization. It will fail procurement review.
A is wrong. Laptops create a worse security posture. They have no central logging and no patch control. They do not dodge the requirement for agency systems.

heading: Q41
question:
Before launching a customer-facing financial advice assistant, the risk team orders pre-launch safety testing. The assistant must refuse disallowed requests (for example instructions to commit fraud), must not leak internal data, and must stay in its role under adversarial users.

The testing must actively try to break the safety controls. You must document residual risks for sign-off. Do not hide residual risks.

Which two elements belong in the pre-launch safety plan? (Select two.)

choices.A: A marketing review of the assistant's greeting messages.
choices.B: Load testing to 10x expected traffic.
choices.C: An adversarial test set: jailbreak attempts, fraud-request phrasings, and role-confusion probes, run against the system with pass/fail grading.
choices.D: A residual-risk register: documented known weaknesses, their severity, mitigations in place, and explicit sign-off by risk owners.

explanation:
Why C, D is correct: C does red-teaming: it actively attacks the controls, which the constraint requires. D is governance: write down residual risks with severity and sign-off instead of discovering them after launch. Testing finds the holes. The register makes them a managed decision.
A is about tone, not safety controls. It does not try to break anything.
B is a reliability activity. It is valuable but unrelated to the safety-testing constraint.

heading: Q42
question:
A public benefits assistant answers questions about government programs. Users act on its answers. They apply for benefits. They appeal denials. A user advocate group asks for transparency. People must know they talk to AI.

They must know where answers come from. They must have recourse when answers are wrong.

Constraint: users must be able to tell it is AI, verify its claims, and challenge wrong answers.

Which transparency design satisfies all three?

choices.A: Clear AI disclosure at conversation start, citations linking each factual claim to its source document, and a visible appeal path (human review request) for disputed answers.
choices.B: Publishing the system prompt so users can see how it works.
choices.C: A disclaimer that the assistant "may make mistakes" with no other changes.
choices.D: A small "AI assistant" label in the footer of the page.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Each constraint maps to one element. Upfront disclosure tells users it is AI. Per-claim citations let them verify. The appeal path gives recourse. All three together make transparency operational rather than decorative.
D is wrong. A footer label is easy to miss. It provides no verifiability or recourse.
B is wrong. Publishing the prompt exposes internals. It does not help users verify any specific answer.
C is wrong. A generic disclaimer shifts blame to the user. It provides no verification or appeal.

heading: Q43
question:
A department head asks for an AI. The AI must make the team smarter. The architect has a kickoff meeting next week. The architect must make buildable requirements from this request.

Constraint: leave the meeting with specific users, tasks, and measurable success criteria, not vibes.

What does structured discovery look like here?

choices.A:
Run a structured session. Identify the users. Identify tasks that take much time today. Define what good looks like with numbers. Identify existing data. Identify what must not happen.

Write this as agreed requirements.
choices.B: Ask for the budget first; requirements follow the money.
choices.C: Build a quick prototype and iterate until the stakeholder stops complaining.
choices.D: Demo the most impressive model capabilities and let the stakeholder pick favorites.

explanation:
Why A is correct: Structured discovery changes "make us smarter" into requirements. It defines users, tasks, metrics, data, and guardrails. The written requirements become the contract. People judge the build against this contract. This meets the demand.
D is wrong because demos anchor stakeholders on flashy capabilities. They do not anchor stakeholders on their actual tasks.
B is wrong because budget without requirements just buys an expensive unguided build.
C is wrong because prototype-and-complain is discovery by accident. It is slow and unbounded. It never produces agreed success criteria.

heading: Q44
question:
The architecture team must choose between two designs. The designs are for an executive briefing. Design A has 96 percent accuracy. It has 4-second latency. It has a higher cost. Design B has 91 percent accuracy.

It has 1.2 seconds latency. It has a lower cost. The executives are not technical.

Constraint: executives must understand the trade-off well enough to make the call, in one page.

How should the architect present the decision?

choices.A: A 20-slide deck on transformer internals so they appreciate the complexity.
choices.B: Make one page. Show the business goal. Show both options. Include accuracy, latency, and cost numbers side by side. Show what each option risks. Give a clear recommendation with reasons.
choices.C: Recommend Design A without mentioning Design B, to keep it simple.
choices.D: Let the executives vote after a live demo of both.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Non-technical decision-makers need the trade-off in business terms. They need the goal, options with comparable numbers, risks, and a recommendation. One page forces clarity. It gives them everything they need to decide.
A is wrong because internals do not help a business decision. They bury the decision.
C is wrong because hiding the alternative removes the decision. It is a sales pitch. It is not architecture communication.
D is wrong because demos show best cases. They do not show trade-offs. A vote without numbers is theater.

heading: Q45
question:
A consulting firm hands a finished Claude agent to the client's internal team. Three months later the client team cannot debug a failure: they do not know the prompts, the eval results, or the intended operating limits.

Constraint: the receiving team must be able to operate, debug, and extend the system without the original builders.

What should the handoff documentation have contained?

choices.A: The source code only; good code documents itself.
choices.B: A one-page marketing summary of what the agent does.
choices.C: The final demo video and the invoice.
choices.D: Show the architecture overview. Show all prompts and their versions. Show eval sets and latest scores. Show known limitations and operating limits. Show the runbook for common failures. Show onboarding steps for new maintainers.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Operating an LLM system requires its prompts, evals, limits, and runbooks. It does not just require code. D is the complete package. It lets a new team debug ("what changed?"). It lets them know the limits ("what is it not for?"). It lets them extend safely.
C is wrong because a demo video shows the happy path. An invoice shows the price. Neither helps debugging.
A is wrong because prompts, evals, and limits are the actual behavior contract of an LLM system. Code alone omits them.
B is wrong because marketing copy contains zero operational information.

heading: Q46
question:
Sales promises a client. The support bot will resolve 95 percent of tickets automatically. The pilot data shows 78 percent resolution. The other tickets need humans. People draft the contract now.

Constraint: the SLA in the contract must be achievable and measurable, or the company will pay penalties.

What should the architect do about the SLA?

choices.A: Refuse the contract entirely.
choices.B: Accept the 95 percent SLA; the model will improve with more data.
choices.C: Push back with pilot data: propose a tiered SLA (for example 80 percent auto-resolution with defined response times for the human-handled remainder), measured monthly with a clear definition of "resolved."
choices.D: Sign the 95 percent SLA but define "resolved" loosely so it is easy to hit.

explanation:
Why C is correct: The pilot data shows the 95 percent figure is not true. A tiered, measurable SLA uses real numbers. This SLA protects both sides. It has achievable targets. It handles the remainder explicitly. Defining "resolved" exactly prevents gaming.
B is wrong. "will improve" is a hope. It is not a basis for a penalty-bearing contract.
D is wrong. A loosely defined metric is dishonest. It will fail at the first client audit.
A is wrong. It abandons the deal. It does not negotiate an honest SLA.

heading: Q47
question:
Users keep reporting that the HR policy bot gives outdated answers after policy updates. There is no channel for these reports except angry emails to the HR inbox, which nobody routes to the engineering team.

Constraint: user-reported issues must reach the team and trigger a fix cycle, repeatedly.

Which feedback-loop design closes this gap?

choices.A: The product gives feedback on every answer. The feedback can be helpful, outdated, or wrong. A team reviews a triage queue at a fixed time. A policy-update process refreshes the knowledge source. The process re-runs evaluations before it publishes.
choices.B: Retrain the model monthly on all HR emails.
choices.C: Remove the bot until policies stop changing.
choices.D: Tell users to email a new support address.

explanation:
Why A is correct: The loop has four parts. A builds all four parts. It builds capture (in-product feedback). It builds routing (triage queue with cadence). It builds fix (knowledge refresh). It builds verification (re-run evals).
A report cannot reach the team. A report cannot trigger a fix. This is not a loop.
D is wrong. A new inbox has no triage cadence. It has no fix process. This is the same gap with a different address.
B is wrong. Retraining on raw emails is slow. It is expensive. It does not target the actual problem (stale knowledge).
C is wrong. Policies always change. Waiting for stability means you never ship.

heading: Q48
question:
A demo of the new claims assistant wows the operations leaders: it handles the five demo claims flawlessly. They now expect the same on all 40 claim types starting Monday. The architect knows the eval set only covers 12 types at 88 percent accuracy.

Constraint: align expectations with measured reality before launch, without killing the project.

What is the right expectation-setting move?

choices.A: Cancel the project; the gap is too large.
choices.B: Quietly expand the eval set over the weekend and launch anyway.
choices.C: Launch Monday as expected; the demo proves it works.
choices.D: Present the eval results plainly: 12 of 40 types covered at 88 percent, the rest untested. Propose a phased rollout starting with the covered types, with expansion gated on eval coverage.

explanation:
Why D is correct: This is honesty with a path forward. The evaluation numbers set the real expectation. The phased rollout changes the gap into a plan. It does not make it a surprise. Leaders get a launch. It is a scoped launch.
It connects to evidence.
C is wrong. The demo covered five hand-picked claims. Launching on 40 untested types guarantees a painful surprise.
A is wrong. Phasing can manage the gap. Cancellation wastes the working 12 types.
B is wrong. A weekend evaluation expansion is too fast. You cannot verify it. It hides the risk. It does not manage the risk.

heading: Q49
question:
The provider deprecates the model version. This model version powers a production assistant. The provider gives 90 days notice. The assistant's prompts work with the old version's behavior. The team did not run a version migration before.

Constraint: migrate without a quality regression, with a rollback option if the new version underperforms.

Which lifecycle plan meets the constraint?

choices.A: Switch the model ID on deprecation day; the new version is strictly better.
choices.B: Pin the old version until the last day, then switch overnight.
choices.C: Run the frozen eval set against the new version now. Fix prompt or config gaps until scores match. Shadow-deploy (the new version handles a copy of traffic, outputs compared). Cut over gradually with the old version as instant rollback. Document the new baseline.
choices.D: Rewrite all prompts from scratch for the new version without testing the old ones first.

explanation:
Why C is correct: Every element helps the constraint. Eval comparison proves no regression before cutover. Shadow deployment tests with real traffic. It does not affect the user. Gradual cutover with rollback limits the blast radius. The documented baseline helps the next migration.
A is wrong. "Strictly better" is not proven for this workload. Behavior changes break tuned prompts.
B is wrong. It puts all risk into one overnight switch. There is no evidence. There is no rollback rehearsal.
D is wrong. Discarding tuned prompts without testing wastes good work. It adds unmeasured risk.

heading: Q50
question:
Security wants to lock down the new agent. Security wants three months for review. Product wants the agent live next week. This will help to hit a revenue target. Both groups escalate to the architect. The standoff blocks the launch.

Constraint: Do not ignore either side's core need. Do not expose unreviewed risk. Do not miss the revenue window. Make a conscious decision if you miss the revenue window.

How should the architect resolve the conflict?

choices.A: Risk-tiered rollout: launch next week to a limited internal pilot with the highest-risk tools disabled and full logging. Complete the security review against real pilot data. Then expand in stages as reviewers approve controls.
choices.B: Launch fully but promise security a review next quarter.
choices.C: Side with product; revenue pays for security later.
choices.D: Side with security; delay the launch three months.

explanation:
Why A is correct: The tiered rollout respects both constraints. Product gets a live launch on schedule. This is a scoped launch. Security gets a review before broad exposure. Real pilot data makes the review better than a theoretical review. Neither side's main need is lost.
C is wrong. It ignores security's main need. Unreviewed exposure is what the constraint forbids.
D is wrong. It ignores product's main need. It does not find a middle path.
B is wrong. A promised future review is not a control. It is the unreviewed exposure. The constraint forbids this.

heading: Q51
question:
A financial guidance assistant told a user to take an action that cost them money. The advice was wrong. The user now threatens legal action. The team contained the incident (they disabled the bad answer pattern). Leadership asks for the post-incident plan.

Constraint: respond honestly to the affected user, prevent recurrence, and preserve trust with all stakeholders.

Which two actions are essential? (Select two.)

choices.A: A stakeholder communication plan shows what to tell the affected user. It shows what to tell leadership and legal. It shows what changes users will see. Legal must review the plan before release.
choices.B: Immediately delete all logs of the incident to limit legal exposure.
choices.C: Publicly blame the model provider for the bad advice.
choices.D: A blameless postmortem shows the timeline. It shows the root cause. It shows why the wrong advice passed every check. It shows fixes with owners and dates. It shows evaluation additions. This tests the failure class forever.

explanation:
Why D, A is correct: D prevents recurrence. Root cause plus permanent eval coverage means this failure type cannot return silently. A handles the human side. Honest, legally reviewed communication to the affected user and stakeholders keeps trust. Technical fix and communication are both necessary. One without the other fails the constraint.
B is wrong. It is probably unlawful. Destroying evidence during a legal action makes worse liability. This liability is worse than the incident itself.
C is wrong. Blame-shifting destroys trust. It does nothing to prevent recurrence.

heading: Q52
question:
A pipeline classifies 2 million customer messages per month into 8 fixed categories. The task is simple pattern matching; a small model already scores 97 percent on the eval set, above the 95 percent SLA.

Constraint: Meet the 95 percent SLA. Do this at the lowest cost and latency. No extra quality is necessary.

Which model choice is correct?

choices.A: Alternate between models randomly to compare them in production.
choices.B: The mid-tier model, as a compromise between the other two.
choices.C: The largest model, for maximum quality headroom.
choices.D: The smallest, fastest model that clears the SLA (already verified at 97 percent), since extra quality beyond the bar buys nothing.

explanation:
Why D is correct: Model selection is a trade-off decision against the SLA. The small model already clears 95 percent. So, it meets the quality bar at the lowest cost and latency. Paying for headroom that nobody needs breaks the cost constraint.
C is wrong. Unused quality headroom at 2M messages per month is pure cost.
A is wrong. Random alternation is not an evaluation method. It only adds inconsistency.
B is wrong. "Compromise" without measurement is not a selection criterion. The cheaper option already meets the SLA.

heading: Q53
question:
A data-extraction prompt asks the model to return JSON with specific fields, but the model keeps returning slightly different field names and formats. The instruction "return JSON" is in the prompt, with zero examples.

Constraint: the output format must be exactly right on every call, since a parser consumes it.

Which prompting technique fixes the format drift?

choices.A: Chain-of-thought reasoning, so the model thinks harder about the format.
choices.B: Few-shot prompting: include 3 to 5 input-output examples showing the exact JSON schema, so the model imitates the format precisely.
choices.C: Zero-shot with a longer explanation of what JSON is.
choices.D: Raise the temperature for more creative formatting.

explanation:
Why B is correct: Format compliance is a pattern-matching task. Few-shot examples show the exact pattern to copy. Three to five examples define field names, nesting, and types. They do this better than prose instructions.
A is wrong. Chain-of-thought helps reasoning. It does not help format adherence. It can even add extra text around the JSON.
C is wrong. The model already knows what JSON is. The problem is which schema. Prose cannot define this.
D is wrong. Higher temperature increases format variance. This is the opposite of the goal.

heading: Q54
question:
A team writes its first system prompt for a refund-policy assistant. The draft is three paragraphs of background about the company, ending with "answer refund questions helpfully."

Constraint: the prompt must reliably produce accurate, policy-grounded answers in a consistent format.

What belongs in a well-designed system prompt here?

choices.A: A friendly persona with jokes, to make answers engaging.
